title: What the lichens said
bodyMd:
A lichen is not a single organism but a partnership: a fungus that gives it structure, and a photosynthesising partner, usually an alga, that supplies food. Because a lichen has no roots and no waxy skin, it takes in water and dissolved substances over its whole surface, straight from rain and air. This makes it an excellent sponge for nutrients and, unfortunately for the lichen, for pollutants.

In the nineteenth century, naturalists noticed that lichens were scarce in and around industrial cities and abundant in the countryside. The pattern was later tied, largely, to sulphur dioxide, a gas released when coal and oil containing sulphur are burned. Some species tolerate a good deal of it; others vanish at very low concentrations. By recording which species grew on tree trunks at a series of sites, scientists could rank the sites by air quality without a single gas measurement, using nothing more than a hand lens, a field guide and a patient afternoon.

When emissions of sulphur dioxide fell sharply in many European countries from the 1970s onward, sensitive lichens began to return to city trees. The recovery has been slower than hoped, however, and it has not been uniform. Species that thrive on nitrogen, which comes in particular from vehicle exhausts and agricultural ammonia, have spread at the expense of others. A tree in a clean-air city can now be as crowded with lichens as a tree in the countryside and yet be crowded with different ones.

This has changed what lichens are asked to say. A survey that once asked only how much sulphur dioxide was in the air must now ask about several pollutants at once, and the answer is read from the make-up of the whole community rather than from the presence or absence of a single species. The method is still cheap, but it has become less like a thermometer and more like a medical examination.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph science passage of about 320 words titled "What the lichens said". The first paragraph explains that a lichen is a partnership of a fungus and a photosynthesising partner, usually an alga, and that with no roots or waxy skin it absorbs water and dissolved substances over its whole surface, so it soaks up both nutrients and pollutants. The second paragraph says nineteenth-century naturalists noticed lichens were scarce near industrial cities, later tied largely to sulphur dioxide from burning sulphur-containing coal and oil; species differ in tolerance, and scientists could rank sites by air quality just by recording species on tree trunks, using only a hand lens, a field guide and a patient afternoon. The third paragraph says that when sulphur dioxide emissions fell sharply in many European countries from the 1970s, sensitive lichens began to return, slowly and unevenly, while nitrogen-loving species, fed by vehicle exhausts and agricultural ammonia, spread at others' expense, so a clean-air city tree can be as crowded with lichens as a countryside tree yet with different ones. The fourth paragraph says surveys must now consider several pollutants and read the whole community rather than a single indicator species; the method is still cheap but more like a medical examination than a thermometer.
